messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert, a 71-year-old security guard who had worked the same quiet evening shift for nearly a decade, was on duty at a suburban community center when a lone gunman—later determined to have ties to an extremist group—opened fire during a senior citizens’ bingo night. That evening, Robert’s job was to check IDs at the main entrance, but he was overwhelmed when the first shots rang out from the hall behind him. He froze, then ducked behind a pillar, unable to move toward the attacker or to guide the panicked crowd. He remembers the smells of cordite and spilt coffee, the wet thud of bodies, and the long, stretched quiet after the final shot. But when he tries to describe what happened next, the sequence blurs: he can picture a shoe, a shattered glass case, a woman’s hand on the floor, but he cannot arrange them in time. Sometimes, when he forces himself to talk about it, his voice goes flat and the images feel distant, as if they belong to someone else—a sensation that leaves him both haunted and oddly disconnected from his own past.

Right after the attack, Robert could not shake the feeling that he should have acted differently. He became convinced that someone else in his position would have charged the gunman or at least shouted a warning, and that he had failed in his most important duty: protecting others. These appraisals cut into him daily. He began to believe he could not handle even minor stressors—a loud noise, a raised voice—without falling apart. To cope, he adopted a rigid set of habits. At his security post, he now positions his chair against the far wall, scanning the entire room with his back protected. At home, he does the same at the dinner table, to his wife’s quiet dismay. He spends hours mentally rehearsing how he would get even with the assailant, imagining confrontations and acts of vengeance that loop endlessly but never soothe him. And he remains hypervigilant toward every person who enters his line of sight, cataloging their hands, their jackets, their pace.

These strategies, however, feed back into his memory. Sitting with his back to the wall and scanning for threats keeps his mind in the same high-alert state as during the attack, which triggers vivid, unbidden recollections—the smell of cordite, the flat echo of shots—yet paradoxically, the more he tries to protect himself, the more fragmented his story becomes. The vengeful fantasies and constant vigilance also reinforce his sense of inadequacy: each time he checks a stranger’s hands, he silently tells himself that a truly capable guard would not need such precautions, that real strength would have meant acting that night. His hypervigilance, meant to restore control, only confirms his belief that he cannot manage even the slightest uncertainty. By now, Robert has cut back his shifts to the bare minimum and avoids the community center entirely, telling his supervisor he prefers the smaller parking-garage detail. His wife says he has become distant, lost in loops of replay and resentment. He sought help only after she threatened to leave, and he now sits in the clinic’s waiting room with his back pressed against the wall, unsure whether he wants to get better or just to stop feeling so ashamed.
